stories.title: Taoiseach says world has 'failed Palestine' in UN address
stories.summary: The Taoiseach has said that when the true horrors of Gaza "are finally and fully revealed, it will shame the world". During his address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Micheál Martin said the international community has "failed Palestine" and criticised last year's Gaza peace plan, saying that it has not "changed the reality on the ground". "When the full truth of what has happened - what is still happening - in Gaza is finally known, when the evidence is gathered, when the testimonies are heard, when the true horrors are finally and fully revealed, it will shame the world," he said as the audience applauded. Mr Martin also hit out at attempts to make the prospect of a two-state solution "impossible". "It is the stated intent of the Prime Minister of Israel, who said clearly that 'we are going to fulfil our promise that there will be no Palestinian state. This place belongs to us,' as he permitted the E1 settlement development in East Jerusalem." The Taoiseach said that most countries have taken steps to push back against "the illegal and violent settler occupation of Palestinian land in the West Bank", but he said time is running out.

stories.title: Single homeless adults 'overlooked', warns charity
stories.summary: Simon Communities of Ireland has warned that single adults have been largely overlooked in housing policy and homelessness responses, despite being the dominant demographic living in emergency accommodation. The most recent figures from the Department of Housing show 61% of all adults living in emergency accommodation are classed as "single". This figure includes childless couples, but very many adults are experiencing homelessness on their own. "We simply won't end homelessness if we are not talking about this cohort and putting targeted resources behind it," said Ber Grogan, Executive Director of Simon Communities of Ireland. As well as representing 61% of all adults in emergency accommodation, single adult homelessness has increased by 61% in the last five years, climbing from 4,501 in July 2021 to 7,244 in July 2026. Tackling this is the focus of Simon Communities of Ireland's first national fundraising campaign: Homeless & Alone: One Big Push.

stories.title: Seanad bye-election to be announced
stories.summary: Minister for Housing and Local Government James Browne is to confirm a bye-election for the remaining vacancy in the Oireachtas. He will move the writ for the contest to fill a seat on the Seanad's Cultural and Educational panel, which has been vacated since Fine Gael's Sean Kyne returned to the Dáil after winning the Galway West bye-election in May. The close of nominations for the ballot is Tuesday, 6 October, with ballot papers to be issued to those voting on Friday, 23 October. The poll closes on Friday, 6 November. There are 234 members of the Dáil and Seanad who are eligible to vote, of which 51.2% are representatives of Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael. Former Dublin City Lord Mayor Ray McAdam has been selected as the Fine Gael candidate, having seen off competition from Kilkenny Councillor David Fitzgerald, Laois Councillor Vivienne Phelan, Sligo Councillor Thomas Walsh and Galway Councillor Frank Fahy, among others. The Cavan native and Dublin City Councillor ran unsuccessfully in the Dublin Central bye-election in May to fill the seat of his party colleague Pascal Donohue, receiving 10.67% of the vote.

stories.title: Almost €1.7 billion in mortgages approved in August, BPFI
stories.summary: Banks are reporting that last month was the strongest in 15 years for mortgage approvals in Ireland, according to the Banking and Payments Federation of Ireland (BPFI). More than 5,000 property loans were given the green light in August valued at nearly €1.7 billion. BPFI said mortgage lending volumes were up12% year on year and values were up by 15%. First-time buyers remained the main driver of activity, accounting for almost 60 per cent of approvals during the month. While there were 55,854 mortgage approvals in the twelve months to August 2026. These were valued at almost €18.1 billion, exceeding €18 billion for the first time.

stories.title: Reporters regain White House access after Trump ban
stories.summary: The White House has said it has reinstated journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico after a federal judge deemed US President Donald Trump's ban of the three news outlets likely unconstitutional and ordered their access immediately restored. The midday reinstatement came after a chaotic few hours earlier when the journalists continued to be blocked from entering the White House grounds. That prompted the three news organisations to request an immediate hearing before US District Judge Tim Kelly, who issued his decision overnight. Judge Kelly, acting in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Monday, ordered a halt to Mr Trump's ban for 14 days in a press freedom case that has played out over the past week in the courtroom and White House grounds. Judge Kelly found that the revocation of the White House credentials of the journalists "likely violated their constitutional due process rights". The judge, who Mr Trump appointed in 2017 during his first presidential term, also raised doubts about the US Justice Department's national security arguments for justifying the ban, noting that Mr Trump himself had said the action was due to what the president alleged was false or negative coverage. Hours after Kelly issued his order, CNN, MS NOW and Politico told the judge they remained barred, and asked for the emergency hearing. Politico said its reporter's credentials were confiscated. An MS NOW reporter said she was blocked from the White House. CNN said some of its staff members were denied entry onto the grounds.

stories.title: New faces and differing form makes for exciting cup final
stories.summary: This year's Club Orange Women's FAI Cup final will be another showcase of one of the biggest rivalries in Irish sport right now. Sunday sees Shelbourne return to the decider, while Athlone Town look to retain the trophy. Although last season Athlone had to beat Bohemians to get their hands on the cup, this year's finalists have faced off in three of the last four deciders. The league has been a similar story, with the pair fighting it out for the title year after year. The two clubs know each other inside out, but some big turnover in players and management, along with differing recent form, makes for a potentially exciting clash. John Russell, who was appointed Shels manager in November last year, has led his team back to the cup final after missing out last year.

stories.title: Byrnes, Hegarty and Hayes up for Hurler of the Year
stories.summary: All-Ireland champions Limerick lead the way with 13 nominations for this year's PwC All-Stars, while the Treaty men also have two players vying for Hurler of the Year. Two former winners - Diarmaid Byrnes (2022) and Gearóid Hegarty (2020) - will go up against Cork attacker Brian Hayes for the individual award. Limerick reclaimed the Liam MacCarthy Cup this summer to complete a clean sweep, having landed the Munster and Allianz League crowns earlier in the year. Eight counties are represented in the nominations, with beaten All-Ireland finalists Galway next on the list with 11 players. Cork have seven, followed by three for fellow semi-finalists Clare, while quarter-finalists Dublin and Offaly have three and two nominations respectively. Neighbours Waterford (two) and Kilkenny (one) finish out the list. Two Galway players are going for the Young Hurler of the Year award. They are Jason Rabbitte and Cillian Trayers, with Cork's William Buckley the third player to be involved.

stories.title: Team news: Abankwah gets nod to start in Kosovo
stories.summary: Udinese defender James Abankwah has been named to start in a rejigged back five for the Republic of Ireland's UEFA Nations League opener against Kosovo at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium in Pristina. With captain Nathan Collins injured and the unattached Séamus Coleman opting not to take up a spot in the squad for this window, Heimir Hallgrimsson has been prompted to alter his favoured back-line. Longford man Abankwah, in his first competitive start for the Boys in Green, and Everton's Jake O’Brien are poised to fill the right side of the back five, while Liam Scales starts ahead of Ryan Manning at left wing back. John Egan and stand-in captain Dara O'Shea take on central defensive berths in front of Ireland number one Caoimhin Kelleher. Jayson Molumby is joined in the heart of midfield by Jason Knight with Finn Azaz and Chiedozie Ogbene playing off centre forward Troy Parrott. Jimmy Dunne is the only squad member missing from the substitutes’ bench after sustaining a knock.

stories.title: Exciting O'Shea can offer hope to injury-plagued Munster
stories.summary: The United Rugby Championship gets underway this weekend, and after a full pre-season programme and a number of competitive friendlies, most squads will feel they have done everything possible to prepare for the opening round. For Munster, however, the start of the season comes with a familiar problem, injuries. Their list of unavailable players remains significant, with Jack Crowley, Jeremy Loughman, Tom Farrell and Calvin Nash among those sidelined, while others like Shane Daly are managing shorter-term issues. It means Clayton McMillan and his coaching staff are having to navigate the opening rounds without a number of high-quality players who would ordinarily be central to their plans. Munster open their campaign on Saturday evening at Thomond Park against Glasgow Warriors, a side capable of testing every part of the home team's game. Glasgow bring physicality, speed and a level of consistency that has made them one of the most difficult teams to contain in the URC. There was genuine excitement around Tom Wood last season. The young, talented out-half made his debut off the bench against Glasgow back in January in Scotstoun. Despite losing the game, there were positive signs of uncovering another gem in the out-half position. Supporters got excited about Tom Wood's future in red. He went on to lead the Ireland Under-20’s in their Six Nations campaign. With Jack Crowley injured, the young out-half was given an opportunity to step into a more significant role throughout pre-season. However, his management of a shoulder injury has unfortunately caught up with him and he’s been forced into a surgical procedure to fix the problem for the long-term.

stories.title: Rebellious Hope - seven dancers defy the rules of ageing
stories.summary: For this year's Dublin Theatre Festival, celebrated choreographer Phillip Connaughton brings seven internationally acclaimed performers aged from 46–86 years and musician Mel Mercier together for an electrifying new live work celebrating resilience, vulnerability and defiance - Phillip introduuces Rebellious Hope below. Even as dancers, from a very early age we are conditioned to prepare ourselves for an early retirement. Whether we want to or not, it often seems like the right thing to do. Of course, we live in a youth-obsessed world, so when I turned 50 last year, it suddenly seemed important to ask myself: what next? I'd never done that before. It was the first time I’d ever questioned my career as a dancer. Looking to the future, I wasn’t sure if there was still space for this body of mine that had dedicated its whole life to dance. I decided to make a short dance documentary for Bealtaine Festival called Rebellious Hope, where I questioned a group of dance artists that I really admire — all of them between the ages of 46 and 86 years old, and all still performing internationally at the top of their game. My question to these incredible artists was simple: What is it that makes you keep dancing? Society tells us that the ageing body has less value. That these older dancers are somehow less interesting. But society is wrong. As dancers age, they carry their personal history in their bodies. And as they learn to navigate the changes that come with ageing, they have to hone all of their skills in order to find new pathways of expressing things that, perhaps, a younger body can express through sheer strength. In my humble opinion, this honing of skills, this economy of movement, this depth of experience, makes the virtuosity of youth seem rather crass.

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (September 25-27)
stories.summary: From pop-up fashion on Grafton Street to sensory-friendly screenings in Raheny, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. Woven Relations pop-up is a free event that brings an array of early-career designers together under one roof in Bewley's Grafton Street from 11am-5pm on Saturday, 26 September. Among them will be Lainey Whelan's hand-printed tights brand, T-Lainey, which has been worn onstage by award-winning singer CMAT. Attendees can purchase one-of-a-kind pieces and get to know the faces and minds behind their next favourite designers, such as Conor O’Brien Studio, Casa Cor and Moroccan brand Anouri Original. Sensinema brings a screening of The Secret of Kells to St Anne's Park, Raheny, on Saturday, 26 September 2026. Located by the Red Stable Carpark, there will be pre-screening music and chats from 3pm, with the film beginning at 4pm. Get event access guide here. Running from 24 September — 11 October, 18 days of theatre will take place all around Dublin. From world premieres and major Irish productions to extraordinary international work, some of the most exciting artists making theatre today are coming to Dublin this year. The Dublin Festival of History will run from 26 September to 11 October 2026, shining a fresh perspective on history and its importance in our everyday lives. Attracting best-selling Irish and international historians to Dublin for a high-profile programme of history talks and debate each Autumn, the festival is now celebrating its 14th year. Check out the full programme of events here. On the last Thursday of every month, Dublin stays open later. Museums, galleries, shops, cafés and venues across the city push their closing time back and put on something extra – exhibitions, live music, workshops, late openings, and the odd thing you won't see coming. See the full line-up of events here.

stories.title: Gaza puts Israel and its critics centre stage at UN
stories.summary: I’m not just talking about the endless NYPD cops, hundreds of armed Secret Service officers with sniffer dogs, nor the near-constant ringing of sirens from motorcades flooding down the streets. Also popping up around the city were striking advertisements on trucks and billboards. This was one of the ways in which Israel was making its presence felt around the city, with hundreds of billboards and digital trucks carrying messages focused on Iran and its nuclear programme, as well as the US-Israel relationship. Israel and its involvement in US strikes on Iran, its actions in Gaza and the Occupied West Bank were central to many of the conversations and discussions happening at the UN. And Israel wanted to put forward its narrative, during a week when it was facing even more criticism. Those concerns being raised were echoed in the Taoiseach's speech to the United Nations General Assembly last night.

stories.title: Call for supports to stop 'spiral' of teen criminality
stories.summary: The chairperson of a children's residential and aftercare group has said early supports are needed for families whose children are involved in anti-social behaviour and crime to prevent crime "spiralling" further. Terry Dignan of the Children’s Residential and Aftercare Voluntary Association, Crava, and director of Don Bosco Care said that there should be "balance" when addressing youth crime. Five teenagers were killed when the car they were travelling in, which was going the wrong way down the motorway, crashed into an oncoming car on 16 August. Three women and a child who were travelling in the other car were seriously injured. "While everybody recognises the tragedy there for the families, obviously for all concerned, we felt there was no balance in terms of what can the Government do in terms of preventing this from happening rather than reacting to harsher penalties and punishments. "So, we were really looking for balance in looking to see what can be done to prevent these young people spiralling into these criminal actions. And we felt that was missing in the public rhetoric," Mr Dignan said.

stories.title: Anti wrong-way-driving tech may be 10-15 years away - TII
stories.summary: Technology to tackle wrong-way motorway driving could be 15 years away, Transport Infrastructure Ireland has told the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Transport. While the spikes, also known as stingers, have been considered, they are not being used because they are unsafe at speed and emergency responders sometimes need to use the wrong-way ramps, according to TII Director of Network Management Pat Maher. People purposely attempting to drive the wrong way can also just enter the motor way correctly and then turn around, he said. The technology, he said, that will have the biggest impact is "through the use of connected vehicles". This will "allow communication between drivers and control centres", he said, but is only currently available in about 5% of cars. It could take "perhaps 10, perhaps 15 years" before the "broader development within the fleet of these communications technologies will allow immediate transmission of messages and alerts to drivers".

stories.title: Oil prices fall as markets look to Iran truce
stories.summary: Oil prices fell slightly todayas markets weighed the possibility of a truce between the US and Iran against the bombing of Saudi Arabia by Houthi rebels after a week of price spikes. Brent was down 87 cents, or 0.82%, at $105.73 a barrel this morning, while West Texas Intermediate was down $1.56, or 1.65%, at $93.05 a barrel. The sluggish opening was a contrast to a week of volatility when oil prices rose to a one-week high yesterday. Both contracts rose as much as 5%. Brent settled up 3.4% and WTI was 2.7% higher. Brent notched its highest close since September 15. It was the first rise in days for WTI, which was down 13% over the prior six sessions and is down 6.42% for the week, compared with Brent's 2.09% rise. The spread between Brent and WTI is the widest it has been since May at $12.68 when it was over $13. Fears of a US ban on diesel exports that could flood the domestic market are largely responsible for the price bifurcation, given that the two benchmarks usually rise and fall in tandem, despite the US contract usually selling for a discount.

stories.title: Eight killed in wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine
stories.summary: A barrage of Russian drone and missile strikes have hit Ukraine, killing six agricultural workers in the east and two people in the capital, Kyiv, in the latest in an intensifying exchange of attacks. The strikes, which triggered air raid sirens and sent locals scurrying underground for shelter, came after both Kyiv and Moscow were at the United Nations and vowed no let-up in their long-range attacks, dimming any immediate prospects for peace in Europe's worst conflict since World War II. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was in New York seeking more Western military support and stronger sanctions against the Kremlin, accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russian attacks have "reached a new level of intensity", killing at least 200 ordinary people across Ukraine so far this month and leaving 1,234 wounded, according to preliminary UN figures. "What stands out is the frequency of the attacks and the striking range of civilian facilities being impacted: places where people live, work, shop and receive essential services," said the head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU), Danielle Bell. Ukraine has meanwhile stepped up its attack on Russia, again with increasing civilian casualties, in what HRMMU called an "escalatory trend" that was illegal under international humanitarian law.

stories.title: Leinster set for fascinating year in Cullen's final quest
stories.summary: As the new BKT United Rugby Championship begins tonight, we have been checking in on each of the Irish provinces over the last few days to recap their 2025/26 campaigns and get a sense of what the new campaign holds. The final stop on our preview tour is the defending champions Leinster, who are heading into their final season under head coach Leo Cullen. Leinster's season is usually quite uneventful until the final third, but 2025/26 had more twists and turns than usual. A combination of an early-season trip to South Africa, combined with a large contingent of players coming back from the British and Irish Lions tour ensured Leo Cullen’s side endured a tough start, which they eventually ironed out in the mid-section of the campaign. Their injury list, particularly at loosehead prop, plagued them throughout, but they still had enough quality to make their way back to the Champions Cup final in Bilbao. Unfortunately, it was another defeat in that decider to Bordeaux-Begles, albeit this one was a 41-19 hammering, in contrast to some of the previous close calls.

stories.title: Preview: Shedding slow starters tag high on Irish agenda
stories.summary: It's the dawn of the fifth edition of the UEFA Nations League and for the Republic of Ireland, it's been a competition that has offered too few happy memories. The Boys in Green have played 22 matches across its four previous League B group phases and only four of those fixtures have ended in a victory. Indeed, Ireland went entirely winless through the first two editions of the Nations League, and have never finished above - or below for that matter - third place in any group. Slow starts have been an Achilles' heel and that facet has also carried over into qualifying campaigns for World Cups and European Championships. On the road towards not reaching the 2022 and 2026 World Cups, as well as Euro 2024 in between, not a single victory was attained within at least the first two games of any of those campaigns. Meanwhile, in every Nations League to date, Ireland have failed to pick up a win in the first two games.

stories.title: Munster searching for stability both on and off the pitch
stories.summary: With just one day to go until the new BKT United Rugby Championship season kicks off, we are doing a province-by-province breakdown over the next few days to remind you how each of the four Irish sides fared in 2025/26, and what to expect from them this season. Next up on our tour of the provinces is Munster, who will be hoping season two under Clayton McMillan is a little more straightforward than season one. It's rarely dull down at Thomond Park, but the 2025/26 one was a constant rollercoaster, both on and off the pitch. When Clayton McMillan came in last summer, his stated aim for getting Munster back on track was for them to find their middle ground more often, rather than playing either to their ceiling or floor on a weekly basis. By that remit, it wasn’t a success. It started impressively with five URC wins in a row, including a famous 31-14 hammering of Leinster. At the time, McMillan pleaded caution that those results were probably papering over some of the cracks in their performances, and so it proved to be, as they lost seven of their next 10 games leading up to the Six Nations, and crashed out of the Champions Cup in the pool stage.

stories.title: Dolores Keane to join RTÉ Radio 1 Folk Awards Hall of Fame
stories.summary: Keane, who died in March this year, was one of the defining voices of Irish folk and traditional music. She grew up in Caherlistrane, Co Galway, immersed in the sean-nós tradition, and made her first recording for Radio Éireann at the age of five. She co-founded the seminal traditional group De Danann in 1975. The group achieved national and international success during a period of renewed interest in Irish folk and traditional music, releasing classic albums including The Rambling Irishman, Anthem and Ballroom. Keane released her debut solo album, There Was a Maid, in 1978. She gained further popularity in the early 1990s with the albums Dolores Keane and A Lion in a Cage, and also featured on A Woman’s Heart, a collection that became the biggest-selling album in Irish history. Among the songs best associated with Keane are Caledonia and Galway Bay. The Hall of Fame award recognises a person who is no longer living and who made a significant contribution to Irish folk music during their lifetime.

stories.title: Beverly Callard taken ill on Fair City set
stories.summary: Beverley Callard has revealed she became unwell while filming Fair City, with an ambulance called to the set. Speaking in a video shared on Instagram, Callard said: "I've been at work this week, filming the most amazing scenes, really good, great scripts. "Working with people who are so good, but good fun as well. It was all going swimmingly and then today, I’ve no idea what happened to me but I was all ready to start a new scene. "We just sat there, getting ready, about to run lines and I sort of… the only way to explain it is I lost consciousness for a few minutes, maybe 10 minutes, which was very odd." Callard said an ambulance was called as part of protocol on set, but she did not go to hospital after recovering. "An ambulance came, I desperately didn’t want to go to hospital, I recovered and then felt fine again," she said.

stories.summary: Kate Brayden shares her tips on how to make the most of autumn, and all its spooky, cosy, bracing beauty. Samhain season is almost upon us, which means plenty of festivals, cosy fireside activities and prancing around leaves in itchy knitwear (if that's what you’re into) before the winter months make it too cold to function. In Irish culture, the time around Halloween feels especially rich in folklore, whether you pay any heed to ancient Celtic pagan traditions or not. Early literature describes great gatherings and feasts around the new beginnings, and who are we to deny 8th century hobbies? So instead of dreading the onset of winter and everything that comes with it, here are some fantastic ways to embrace this crisp, cosy and festive time of year. Who says festivals are just for summer? Europe’s largest of its kind, Derry Halloween has become a staple of the city’s annual calendar, running this year from 28 October 28 to 1 November. "For a few enchanted days and nights, people transform, tell the tallest of tales, and make the unbelievable seem believable", said the festival's organisers. The North also has the 63rd run of the Belfast Arts Festival slated from 14 October to 8 November. Over 30 venues across the city will feature the best international and homegrown artists in theatre, dance, music, visual arts, literature and film.

stories.title: Dublin Winter Lights in December 'not a U-turn' - DCC
stories.summary: Head of Events at Dublin City Council Tony Smithers has said that the capital's Winter Lights Festival will be running in December as before, but that it is also being extended to the beginning of February, as he insisted that the decision was not a U-turn. The confirmation follows a backlash earlier this week after DCC announced in a press release that it was moving the festival from December to January. The festival began in 2018 and has national and international themes with light projections and installations throughout Dublin city centre in December. Speaking on Morning Ireland today, Mr Smithers said: "To clarify, we were moving our Winter Lights as an extension for the projections and the lights in December." He said usually there would be five weeks of lights and projections and now there will be nine weeks. Mr Smithers said it was never intended that Winter Lights was not going to happen in December, and that the council begins planning its Christmas events from early February onwards.

stories.title: Mark English's achievements celebrated in Co Donegal
stories.summary: A large crowd turned out at Finn Valley Athletics Club in Stranorlar, Co Donegal last night to welcome home European 800m gold medallist Mark English. Club member, English became the first man to win gold for Ireland at the European Athletics Championships, after he won the 800m in Birmingham last month. The 33-year-old from Letterkenny also ran a new personal best of 1:42.78 as he finished sixth in the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest recently. The European gold medallist said that the past six week were "pretty hectic", since his success in Birmingham, adding that the response at home has been "special". "I went back to Spain for some altitude training the morning after the race. I didn't get any sleep, and I was back into the thick of it again. "You're starting to get some messages coming through. You start to see what it means to some people and coming back here to Finn Valley today, back to my home county.

stories.summary: Brussels has told British Prime Minister Andy Burnham that Britain needs to raise tariffs on Chinese cars and align more closely align with EU trade ‌policy to avoid "made in Europe" barriers on key exports, the Financial Times said today. In response to lobbying for equal treatment for British products, the bloc told London its best solution would be to join the EU's customs union, the newspaper ⁠said, citing two people familiar with the matter. "A customs union would solve most of the problems of 'made in Europe’," an EU official told the paper. "And also the question of tariff differences, which leads to fears the Chinese could avoid our tariffs by routing through the UK." Burnham said this week he would make the case for Britain to be considered a "trusted partner" under the bloc's proposed "Made in EU" rules, ‌warning ⁠that the UK's exclusion could damage its car industry. The "Made in Europe" policy aims to curb reliance on Chinese components by prioritising European-made goods – a worry for the British auto industry which feeds parts into EU supply ⁠chains and sells cars across the bloc. The bloc would use every available tool to reduce its "unsustainable" trade deficit with China, European Commission President Ursula von ⁠der Leyen told the European Parliament in her 'State of the Union' address, opens new tab this month.

stories.title: NATO chief says alliance 'ready' for Russia hybrid attack
stories.summary: NATO is "ready" for Russian cyberattacks and other forms of hybrid warfare, the alliance's secretary general has said, urging increased support for Ukraine in response to Moscow's actions. "Russia is doing more and more when it comes to the cyber etc. domain, but... NATO is ready for this," Mark Rutte said. "We have all these response options in place... when it comes to hybrids to make sure that we stay strong," the NATO chief said, urging countries to provide "more support for Ukraine" if they "really want to give a signal to the Russians on every hybrid incident, hybrid attack." European countries have been on high alert for any Russian interference, fearing that Moscow could target Kyiv's Western backers as the Kremlin's invasion of Ukraine drags on into its fifth year. Mr Rutte's remarks came after the Danish Defense Intelligence Service (DDIS) said that Russia would likely carry out more hybrid attacks against targets in the West, while assessing that an outright invasion by Moscow was "highly unlikely" but still possible. Last week, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk also warned of "hybrid" threats from Russia - including drone and missile strikes - against Ukraine's allies.

stories.title: Where is the FAI board during this strange, sad week?
stories.summary: This has been the strangest and saddest international window I can remember. Managerial uncertainty, bad results, pressure from supporters, injuries, rows, all that good stuff that football can throw at you and create noise within a camp can have a normality to it. This feels completely different. It has made me deeply uncomfortable. I have written before that I do not believe these games against Israel should be taking place and my feelings have only hardened as they have approached. Even the Kosovo game last night, a match I would normally sit down and enjoy purely as a football person, felt difficult to separate from what is coming next. I don't care that we lost, and have no strong genuine feelings on how we played or how the game went. Not much interest at all.
stories.rssSummary: If you are angry about the Israel games going ahead, do not build a narrative that the players are somehow responsible for that decision or complicit simply because they pull on an Ireland jersey, writes Eoin Doyle.
